speaker: ivy
lines: Careful, don't splash. I'm Ivy. I look after the pools, and the pools are going cold.
They're two degrees down since the first snow. Everyone keeps telling me it's the weather.
But it isn't. It's the stone dam on the low pool. Somebody's been knocking stones out of it.

speaker: ivy
lines: Whoever comes off the otter slide too fast. I'm not naming any names.
Everyone who slides into the dam knocks a stone loose, and the warm water runs out through the gap.
I've kept these pools for eleven winters, and I'm not losing them to somebody's bit of fun.

speaker: ivy
lines: Then get the temperature off Corm, the raven who sits by the steam. The thermometer's on his rock.
He's sat right next to it for a whole year and never once read it. Make him read it.
I want a proper number, mind, not news.

speaker: ivy
lines: And then Corm, on his rock by the steam. Make him read the thermometer.
I want a number, mind, not something he's heard.

speaker: ivy
lines: Forty-one? Off the thermometer? Corm actually read it?
That's up on last week. The dam's holding. Listen to that steam.
Here, have a warm stone from the bottom of the pool. Keep it in a pocket.
And if you see my sister, don't tell her I was worried.

speaker: ivy
lines: This is from Ilsa, my sister? She sent it with you instead of coming herself.
And don't tell me we don't look alike. Everyone says that.
She'd carry the whole valley on her back before she'd knock on my door. Dried apples, and her good scarf.
Tell her it got here. And tell her to come down herself next time, and I'll feed her.

speaker: ivy
lines: Which house is blue? From down here, it's the one with the green door.
At dusk the steam turns everything up the hill blue, and that one most of all.
Pell, the postmaster, ought to come down and look for himself. He never comes down here.

speaker: ivy
lines: Soak your feet before you go. Everybody's feet are cold this time of year.

speaker: corm
lines: News! You'll be wanting the news. I'm Corm. I hear everything, and I pass it all on.
Word is the bakery in Hollowpine Hamlet is shut. Mind you, word is it's open, too.
And word is the post's stopped. Also that it's running. I've been saying all four since breakfast.

speaker: corm
lines: No idea! That's the trouble. I say what I hear, and I hear everything.
Just once, I'd like to say something and have it be true.

speaker: corm
lines: Checked? I'd have to go and ask people. They look at you funny when you ask.
Hearing's easier. Things you hear come to you.

speaker: corm
lines: Orla, who runs the bakery, would know whether it's open.
And Pell, the postmaster, would know whether the post's running.
Would you ask them for me? Then come back and tell me straight, and I'll pass it on right, for once.

speaker: corm
lines: You're back! With news? No? Orla first, at the bakery. Is it open?
Then Pell, the postmaster. Is the post running?
Then come back to me and tell me slowly. I want to get it right.

speaker: corm
lines: Ask Orla, at the bakery, whether it's open, and Pell, the postmaster, whether the post's running. Then come back to me.

speaker: corm
lines: The bakery's open. The post runs inside the valley, but nothing goes over the pass.
And it's all true? Checked? By somebody who actually asked?
Well! I'll pass that on, every word of it. I could get used to this.
Here, for your trouble. And that's not hearsay, those are real bells.

speaker: corm
lines: The pool temperature? I heard it was freezing. Jory, the mouse, told me so.
Ivy wants a reading? Off the thermometer? Not just what I heard?
Oh, fine. The thermometer's right here. I've never once read it. ...Forty-one.
Tell her it's forty-one. That's the first thing I've ever checked. It felt very strange.

speaker: corm
lines: I've checked things this week. Real, actual things. It's exhausting.
The bakery's open, and the post runs inside the valley. Both true. Somebody asked.
Bring me anything you hear, and I'll check it. Probably.

speaker: jory
lines: I have lived at Kettle Springs my whole life, and I have never once been cold.
The warm pool keeps the chill off me. That is the whole reason I stay.
People tell me the pines are not very far away.
I would like to walk as far as the pines, just once. And then come back.

speaker: jory
lines: The pines are where the cold starts. Everyone says so.
I have never felt it, and I think I would like to know what it is like.
Or perhaps I would not. I am not sure. Would you go first?

speaker: jory
lines: Then would you catch me a fish from the warm pool first? It is for the walk, when I go. A mouse should take a lunch.
And then walk to Pinewind Wood for me. Go first, and have a proper look at it.
Then come back and tell me what it is like, and I will decide.

speaker: jory
lines: And then tell me what they are like. All of it, the cold as well.

speaker: jory
lines: The pines are like that? Tall, and creaking, and the snow is quiet there?
And it was cold, but you came back. You are standing right here in front of me.
And the fish. I have it wrapped in a leaf, ready for the walk. I have checked it twice.
So I think I can go. Not today, but tomorrow. As far as the pines.
Here, this is for going first. I am not very good at saying thank you.

speaker: jory
lines: This morning I put one foot out of the warm pool. And then both of them.
It was cold. I stood there and counted to forty, and then I got back in.
Tomorrow I will count to fifty. And then the pines. You will see.

speaker: tuck
lines: Careful on the planks, there. I'm Tuck. I look after this bridge.
I tie it, I tighten it, and I check it every hour. I don't cross it, mind. That's a different job.
The rope's wearing out, see? Look at the fraying there. One more storm and it'll snap.

speaker: tuck
lines: Hold on. Is that Bram's good rope? From the woodstore by the big pine?
He sent it all the way up here? With you? He hasn't said a word to me in years.

speaker: tuck
lines: Somebody has to stand at this end and watch the knots hold. That's me.
Sable, the fox up at the wind post, says I'm scared. Well, Sable files reports, and I tie knots.
We'll leave it at that.

speaker: tuck
lines: Forty feet, no splices. He measured it before he gave it to you, didn't he?
There we are. Tied, tightened and tested. That'll hold through a storm.
Tell Bram it's still forty feet, not an inch short. He can come up and measure it himself if he likes.
I didn't cross it, you'll notice. I didn't need to.
And here. I found this tied into the old rope years ago. Show it to Bram. He'll know what it is.

speaker: tuck
lines: Nettle Chimney can be climbed? The tall rock face past the bridge? You went up it?
Then there's a way up this ridge that doesn't go over a bridge.
I've never said I wouldn't climb, you know. Only that I wouldn't cross.
Tell Sable I'm thinking about it. Only thinking, mind.

speaker: tuck
lines: I check this bridge every hour. I don't cross it, though. That's a different job.
The wind's up. The rope doesn't mind the wind. It's age it minds.
Watch the planks on your way over. I mean that kindly.

speaker: sable
lines: Sable, at the wind post on Windscar Ridge. I measure the wind here and file a report, whatever it says.
So far, today's report just says 'windy'. That won't do at all.
I need two readings, one high and one low. The kite can get me the high one, up over the crest.
And the lantern ascent will get me the low one. I'll read the wind off the flames as you pass them.

speaker: sable
lines: If I only filed reports on the good days, they wouldn't be reports, would they? They'd be fibs with a stamp on.
Tuck, the marten at the bridge, says the wind will take his bridge one day. I say the rope will go first.
One of us will turn out to be right, and I'll file it either way.

speaker: sable
lines: The kite goes first. Get it up off the crest, above the line of the ridge.
Then run the lantern ascent, gate to gate. I'll watch the flames from here.
Then come back to me, and I'll write it all up.

speaker: sable
lines: The report's still blank, I'm afraid. The kite, above the crest, please.
Then the lantern ascent, up the ridge. Then come back to me.

speaker: sable
lines: The kite reading's forty, gusting. The lanterns say the same, lower down. That's consistent.
Now that's a report worth filing. I'll stamp it twice.
And for the record, the bridge stood up through all of it. Don't tell Tuck I wrote that down.
Here, this is for the readings.

speaker: sable
lines: I've got a new question for you. It's been sitting on my desk for a year.
Nettle Chimney is the tall rock face on this ridge. Nobody's ever tried it, and I'd like it on the record.
Take the chimney scramble up to the top. Then go and tell Tuck, the marten at the bridge, that the face can be climbed.
He won't cross a bridge, but he's never said a word about climbing. Then come and tell me.

speaker: sable
lines: The chimney still isn't on the record. Take the scramble up to the top.
Then go to Tuck, and then come back to me. I'll file it either way.

speaker: sable
lines: It can be climbed, and there's a witness. I'll file that.
And Tuck's thinking about it? Tuck's never thought about anything but knots.
So that's two ways up this ridge now. One for crossers, and one for climbers.
Here, this is for the climb. I'll race you up it next time.

speaker: sable
lines: Forty, gusting. Filed. I file everything.
Somebody keeps lighting the lanterns along the ridge. Good. I like a bit of flicker.
Watch yourself on the crest. The wind doesn't file reports. It just pushes.
